meta.blurb: When Tessa inherits her great-uncle's failing bookshop, she plans to sell it within a week. Then she finds the secret notes he hid for strangers, meets the quiet carpenter who lights the lane's lamps, and learns that some places choose their people.
meta.bible: Tessa Marlowe: a translator of Portuguese novels, thirty-two, tired of city life, clever and stubborn, the heroine. Silas Wren: her great-uncle, who kept the bookshop for forty years and died in the spring; he hid small notes for strangers inside books. Daniel Reyes: a carpenter who lights the lane's lamps every dusk, quiet and kind; words move on the page for him, so reading is slow and hard. Poppy: Daniel's niece, eight, who loves books and gives good advice. Mrs Boyle: Imelda Boyle, who runs the tearoom next door, warm, nosy and generous. Mr Hargrove: Gideon Hargrove, who owns the building, stiff and practical, not a villain. Tobias Finch: an old fisherman who has never read poetry. Marcus Vale: Tessa's former boss, a publisher in the city, who offers her a job. Comma: the grey shop cat. Port Hollin: a small seaside town built up a hill. Lantern Lane: the steep lane of shops, lit by old lamps that Daniel lights by hand each evening, a tradition begun by his grandfather. The shop is named Wren Books. Lantern Night: the book festival Tessa organises in the lane. Voice and tone: warm, gentle and cosy, with small humour; a chaste romance; no villains; the ending is happy and earned.

A1A2: A letter told Tessa that her great-uncle Silas had left her a shop.
The train brought Tessa to Port Hollin, where a man was lighting the lamps.
The shop on Lantern Lane was dusty, and a grey cat slept inside.
Mrs Boyle from the tearoom said that everyone loved Tessa's great-uncle Silas.
Mr Hargrove said the shop owed a lot of money, so Tessa wanted to sell.
In the night a shelf fell, and Daniel came in the morning to mend it.
Daniel found a small note in a book, written for the next reader.
Silas had hidden notes for strangers in many books, so Tessa decided to stay.
Tessa, Mrs Boyle and little Poppy cleaned the shop and sorted the boxes.
Tessa found an old book that showed Silas often gave books away.
Daniel fixed every shelf, but he never read the names on the boxes.
On the first day the shop opened, only a few people came in.
Poppy had an idea: Tessa could choose a book to match each person's feelings.
Old Tobias Finch read the poems Tessa chose, and he cried and smiled.
At night Tessa did her translation work at the counter, and Comma sat nearby.
Marcus Vale called from the city and offered Tessa a big job.
Mr Hargrove came back and said the building was going to be sold.
Tessa told Daniel her problem, and he asked her to help light the lamps.
At dusk Tessa lit one lamp, and Daniel told her about his grandfather.
More people came each week, and the children loved to watch Comma sleep.
Daniel made Tessa a window seat, and Poppy read the card to him.
Tessa asked Daniel kindly, and he said that words move on the page for him.
Tessa said she would read aloud every Thursday night, and Daniel could listen.
On Thursday the neighbours came, and Daniel listened with a happy face.
They walked by the sea, and Tessa said she was tired of her old life.
Tessa waited for Thursdays now, and Mrs Boyle smiled at her.
A big storm broke the roof, and everyone ran to save the books.
In the morning they dried the books by the fire, and their hands touched.
In Silas's old desk, Tessa found a letter with her name on it.
Silas wrote that the shop was a promise, and he hoped Tessa would stay.
Daniel asked Tessa for a book, and she gave him a short, kind story.
Every evening Daniel read a little, and a blue sheet helped him see the lines.
At last Daniel finished a whole chapter, and they had tea and cake.
In autumn the shop paid some of the money it owed, but not enough.
Tessa had a big idea: a book night in the lane with lamps.
The baker, the florist and the teacher all said they would help.
Mr Hargrove said no to the plan, and Tessa became very angry.
Daniel was afraid the lamps would go out forever if the lane was sold.
One cold night under a lamp, Daniel and Tessa kissed for the first time.
Marcus wanted an answer soon, but Tessa had not told Daniel about the job.
Daniel saw the job letter on Tessa's screen, and it hurt him.
Daniel told Tessa to take the job, and then they both said hard words.
Alone with Comma, Tessa read Silas's notes and thought about what home means.
Tessa called Marcus and said no, but she offered to work from the shop.
On festival day the lane filled with people and lamps, but Daniel was not there.
Mr Hargrove came, and in an old book he found a note from Silas.
Mr Hargrove felt moved, and he promised a fair rent for the shop and the lamps.
Daniel came late with a letter he wrote himself and read it aloud.
Tessa said she was staying, and they lit the lamps together.
By spring a new sign hung on the shop, and Daniel was reading.
B1B2: Tessa Marlowe is halfway through a busy morning at her desk when a letter arrives from a solicitor. It says that her great-uncle Silas Wren has died and left her his bookshop on Lantern Lane.
Tessa takes the train to the seaside town of Port Hollin and arrives just as the light is fading. A man with a long brass pole is walking up the steep lane, lighting the old lamps one by one.
The shop is dusty, its shelves lean in all directions, and a grey cat is asleep in the window. The cat, Comma, opens one eye as if she has been waiting for Tessa for years.
Mrs Boyle, who runs the tearoom next door, pours Tessa a cup of tea and will not let her pay for it. She says that Silas lent books to half the town, and that everyone has missed him since spring.
Mr Hargrove, who owns the building, explains that the rent has not been paid for many months. Tessa decides on the spot that she will sell the shop quickly and be back in the city within a week.

That night a shelf falls with a crash, and Tessa wakes to find books scattered across the floor. In the morning Daniel, the carpenter from down the lane, arrives with his toolbox because Mrs Boyle has sent him.
While Daniel is lifting the heavy shelf, a small folded note slips out of one of the books. It says only, “For the next reader,” and Tessa feels strangely moved by it.
She opens more books and finds more notes, each one written by Silas for someone he would never meet. Tessa realises how much of him is still in the shop, and she decides to stay for a month.
Mrs Boyle and eight-year-old Poppy come over to help, and the three of them clean until their hands are grey. They sort the boxes into piles of keepers, sellers and books nobody can name.

Under the counter Tessa finds an old ledger in which Silas wrote the name of every book he sold. Beside many of the names he has written “no charge,” and she understands why the shop never made any money.
Daniel mends the shelves with careful hands and never complains about the work. Tessa notices that he never reads the labels on the boxes and always asks her which one to carry.
On the day the shop reopens, Tessa polishes the windows and puts out a hand-written sign. Only a few people come in all day, and the only sale is a postcard to a tourist.
Poppy sits on the counter and says that people do not really want a book, but a way to feel better. Tessa laughs at first, and then she begins to ask every customer how they feel today.

Old Tobias Finch, who has fished all his life and never read a poem, leaves with a thin book of verse. A week later he comes back with red eyes and a wide smile and asks for another, and soon the whole lane is talking about it.

Tessa still has her translation work to do, so she carries her laptop into the shop and writes late into the night. The wifi is weak and the radiator is cold, but Comma sleeps on the desk and keeps her company.
Marcus Vale, her old boss, telephones from the city and offers her a permanent job as an editor. He wants an answer before winter, and Tessa hears herself say that she will think about it.
Mr Hargrove returns with a grave face and a folded letter. A hotel company wants to buy the whole building, he says, and unless the rent is paid by the end of the year, he will have to sell.

Tessa tells Daniel everything while he is working on a shelf, and he stops and listens with serious eyes. He says that the lane is the heart of the town, and he asks if she would like to help him light the lamps.

At dusk Daniel gives her the long brass pole and shows her how to reach the little flame inside the glass. His grandfather started this round long ago, he explains, and in all that time the lamps have never missed a night.

As the weeks pass, more people come through the door, and the till rings a little more often. Children stop outside every morning to watch Comma sleeping in the window, and many of them end up buying a picture book.

Daniel builds Tessa a window seat from old oak and carries it in without being asked. Poppy has to read the little card that comes with it aloud, because Daniel quickly hands it to her, and Tessa sees the quick look on his face.

Later, when they are alone, Tessa asks him gently whether reading is hard for him. Daniel says that the words slide and swim on the page, and that at school the other children laughed at him until he stopped trying.

Tessa does not say that she feels sorry for him, because she can see that he would hate it. Instead she chalks a notice on a small board saying that every Thursday evening she will read aloud, and Daniel says he might come.

On the first Thursday, neighbours arrive with their own chairs and cushions, and the old stove glows warm. Daniel comes in late and sits at the back, and as Tessa reads, she sees him listening with a smile he does not try to hide.

After the reading they walk along the harbour wall, where the sea is black and the lights of the boats are small. Tessa tells him she left the city because she was tired of working all day without speaking to anyone.

Without quite noticing, Tessa has started to count the days until Thursday. Mrs Boyle, who notices everything, tells her over a plate of scones that she is blushing, and Tessa pretends to be busy with the cat.

One night a storm lifts a corner of the roof, and rain begins to pour down onto the shelves. Daniel is the first to arrive, and soon half the lane is in the shop carrying books to safety in their arms.
At dawn the rescued books are open on every chair, drying in front of the fire. Tessa and Daniel are both soaked and tired, and when their hands touch over a damp page, neither of them moves away.
While she is clearing Silas's old desk, Tessa notices a drawer that does not shut properly. Behind it she finds an envelope with her own name on it, written in his thin, careful hand.

The letter says that a shop is a promise to strangers, and that she should keep it only as long as it makes her happy. He adds that Daniel will pretend he needs no help, and that she should help him anyway.

Tessa visits Daniel's workshop, where the air smells of wood and the floor is thick with shavings. He asks her, rather shyly, for a book he could try, and she chooses a short, kind story with large print.

She also gives him a pale blue sheet of plastic to lay over the page, which some readers find makes the lines calmer. Each evening Daniel reads a little more, slowly and stubbornly, and Tessa has never seen anyone work so hard at a page.

One afternoon Daniel arrives at the shop with the book under his arm and tells her he has finished the first chapter. Tessa makes tea and buys a cake, and for a while they simply sit and smile at each other.
Autumn arrives, and golden leaves blow along the lane and into the doorway. The shop has paid part of its debt, but when Tessa adds up the figures, she sees that it is still a long way from enough.

Late one evening Tessa has an idea, and she draws it on the back of an old receipt. She will hold a book festival in the lane itself, with stalls, readings and every lamp lit, and she will call it Lantern Night.

She tells the neighbours, and to her surprise they say yes at once. The baker will bake, the florist will hang flowers, the teacher will bring her pupils, and Mrs Boyle will serve tea to a thousand people.

Tessa goes to Mr Hargrove and asks him to lend his support to the festival. He shakes his head and says that the shop is a sweet dream, and Tessa leaves the building so angry that Daniel has to walk her home.
On the way, Daniel stops by a lamp and tells her that he is afraid. If the lane is sold, he says, the lamps will go out for good, and his grandfather's work will end with him.
A cold frost has settled on the lane, and the lamps glow like small moons. Daniel takes Tessa's hand under the nearest one, and when she looks up, he kisses her very gently.
Marcus telephones again and says he needs her answer by the end of the week. Tessa hangs up, her heart pounding, and realises that she has not told Daniel anything about the job.
The next morning Daniel comes in with a loaf from the baker and sees an email open on her screen. He reads the first line, which he can do slowly, and his face changes at once.

He tells Tessa quietly that she should take the job, because she deserves a bigger life than this small lane. She says that he has no right to decide that for her, and before long they are both saying things they do not mean.
That evening Tessa sits alone with Comma and the box of Silas's notes. One of them, written in faded ink, says that home is not a place but a lamp somebody leaves lit for you.

Tessa picks up the telephone and tells Marcus that she is grateful but will not be taking the job. She adds that she would still like to translate books for him, and that she can do it perfectly well from a shop.

Lantern Night arrives, and the lane fills with stalls, lanterns, music and the smell of baking. Tessa greets everyone with a bright smile, but all evening she keeps looking for Daniel, and he does not come.

Mr Hargrove walks into the crowd with his hands behind his back and looks around him in surprise. Tobias Finch stands up to read a poem, and as the old man's voice rises, Mr Hargrove opens a book at the nearest stall and finds a note tucked inside.

The note is from Silas, and it was written years ago for a man who would one day be ready to be kind. Mr Hargrove reads it twice, then finds Tessa and says that he will offer a fair lease for the shop and for the lamps.

Just as the clock strikes nine, Daniel appears at the end of the lane with a folded sheet of paper in his hand. He tells Tessa that it took him three weeks to write, that the spelling is poor, and that he will read it aloud anyway.

Tessa tells him that she turned the job down days ago and that she is not going anywhere. Then they take the long brass pole between them and light the lamps together, while the whole lane watches and cheers.

By the following spring a new sign hangs over the door, painted by Daniel with Poppy's help. Inside, he is reading a thick novel by the window, and Tessa has just slipped a fresh note into a book for the next reader.
C1C2: On a grey Tuesday morning, in the middle of a deadline she had been dreading, Tessa Marlowe received a thick envelope from a firm of solicitors in a town she had not visited since childhood. Inside she found a short, formal letter informing her that her great-uncle, Silas Wren, had died in the spring. He had left her everything he owned, which consisted, as far as she could tell, of a bookshop at the top of a steep lane called Lantern Lane.

She travelled to the seaside town of Port Hollin on the slow afternoon train, watching the city thin out into fields and then into a pewter-coloured sea. By the time she reached the foot of the hill, the light was fading, and a figure with a long brass pole was making his unhurried way up the lane. One after another, the old lamps bloomed along the cobbles, and Tessa, who had meant to be cynical about the whole business, found herself standing still and watching.

The shop itself proved to be a crooked, dusty, bewildering place, with shelves that leaned like tired sailors and a smell of paper and old tea. In the window lay a grey cat, who regarded the new owner with the weary dignity of someone who had been left in charge. Tessa, who had inherited a business and a creature she had never met, sat down heavily on a stool and wondered what on earth she was supposed to do with either.

Next door, in a tearoom crowded with doilies and teapots, a large and cheerful woman named Mrs Boyle pressed a cup of tea into Tessa's hands and refused every offer of payment. Silas, she said, had lent books to half the town and never once asked for them back, and the lane had felt hollow since he died. Tessa, who had been prepared to be polite to strangers, discovered that it was surprisingly hard to be polite to people who were clearly grieving.

The following morning Mr Hargrove, the landlord, visited the shop in a stiff grey coat and laid a folder on the counter with the air of a man who dislikes bad news and delivers it anyway. The rent, he explained, was many months overdue, and the shop could not continue unless the debt was settled. Tessa, who had her own life to return to, resolved there and then to sell the business as quickly as the law would allow and to be back at her desk within the week.

In the dead of that first night there was a tremendous crash from the shop below, and Tessa came downstairs to find a whole shelf lying across the floor in a drift of paperbacks. It was the carpenter, a tall and quiet man named Daniel Reyes, who arrived with a toolbox at eight o'clock, having been sent by Mrs Boyle, whose network of intelligence was evidently flawless. He greeted Tessa with grave courtesy, rolled up his sleeves, and began to examine the damage without wasting a word.

As Daniel raised the heavy shelf back into place, a small folded note slipped from between two books and fluttered to the floor. Tessa picked it up, expecting a shopping list or a bill, and found instead a single line in an unfamiliar, careful hand: For the next reader. She stood very still, holding it, with the odd sensation that someone who was no longer there had just handed her a gift.

She began to take books from the shelves one at a time, shaking them gently, and notes began to fall out in dozens, each addressed to someone Silas could never have met. Some were jokes, some were advice, and some were simply a few words of comfort to a stranger who might be having a hard week. By the end of the morning Tessa had abandoned the idea of leaving, for she could no longer imagine selling a place that had been quietly looking after people for so long, and she resolved to stay for a month.

With Mrs Boyle and her eight-year-old neighbour Poppy, who had appointed herself assistant manager, Tessa spent several days sweeping, scrubbing and carrying boxes up and down the narrow stairs. The air filled with dust until all three of them looked like ghosts, and the cat withdrew to the windowsill in evident disgust. By the end of the week, however, the shop had begun to resemble a room in which one might actually wish to sit.

At the back of the shop, in a cupboard under the counter, Tessa discovered an old ledger in which her great-uncle had recorded every book he had ever sold. Beside a surprising number of the entries he had written the words no charge, along with the name of a widow, a student, a lonely sailor or a child without pocket money. She closed the ledger with a small ache of understanding, for it explained at last why such a beloved shop had never been able to pay its rent.

Daniel returned day after day to mend what the years had broken, and Tessa found herself glancing up from her cleaning to watch the patient economy of his movements. She noticed, however, that he never read the labels she had written on the boxes, but always asked her quietly which one he should carry and where it ought to go. It struck her as odd in a man so capable, though she was too tactful to remark on it yet.

On the morning the shop reopened, Tessa polished the windows until they shone, propped a hand-lettered sign against the door, and waited with her heart full of foolish hope. A few curious neighbours drifted in and out, nobody bought anything of consequence, and by the close of the day the only customer she had actually served was a tourist wanting a postcard of the harbour. She locked up in the dusk with the uneasy feeling that gratitude and affection were not, after all, a business plan.

It was Poppy, perched on the counter with her legs swinging, who offered the first useful piece of advice anyone had given her about the shop. People, she said with the serene confidence of an eight-year-old, do not really come in for a book; they come in wanting to feel different, and the book is only the way they do it. Tessa laughed at the idea, then thought about it for most of the evening, and the next morning she began asking every customer how they were feeling.

Tobias Finch, an elderly fisherman with hands like knotted rope, had never read a poem in his life and admitted as much with some embarrassment. Tessa listened to him talk about the sea for ten minutes, then pressed a slim volume of verse into his weathered palm and asked him only to try one page. When he returned a week later, red-eyed and smiling, to ask for another, the news ran along Lantern Lane faster than any gossip, and the doorbell rang more often than it had in years.

Tessa's other life did not vanish simply because she had moved into a dusty flat above a shop, and her translation of a Portuguese novel still had to be finished by the end of the month. She carried her laptop down to the counter each night and worked beneath a single lamp, with the weak internet connection stuttering and the cat keeping watch from the desk. There was a curious comfort in the silence, and she noticed that the sentences she wrote there seemed warmer and more alive than anything she had produced in the city.

Marcus Vale, her old employer and an editor of some importance, telephoned from the city to offer her a permanent position with a generous salary. It was precisely the kind of opportunity she had once dreamed about, and she heard herself saying that she would think it over, though she could not have said exactly what was holding her back. He asked for her answer before winter, and Tessa put down the receiver and sat looking at the shelves, feeling oddly divided between two lives.

Mr Hargrove came to the shop again, this time with a sombre expression and a letter that he handled as though it might scald him. A large hotel company, he confessed, had made an offer for the entire building, and unless the debt was paid by the end of the year, he would have no honourable choice but to accept. Tessa, who had sworn to herself she would not become attached, discovered that the thought made her feel physically ill.

That evening she told Daniel everything, and he laid down his plane and listened without once interrupting, his dark eyes steady. When she had finished, he said that the lane was the beating heart of the town, and that if the shop closed, the whole street would slowly lose its courage. Then, rather unexpectedly, he asked whether she would care to join him at dusk, and learn the work of the lamps.

At the appointed hour Daniel handed Tessa the long brass pole, showed her how to lift the small glass door and reach the wick, and stepped back to watch her try. His grandfather had begun the lamp round before the war, he told her, and in all those decades the lane had never once been left in darkness, not even during the worst storms. When the first lamp caught under her careful hand, she felt a quiet, absurd joy, as though she had been admitted to some ancient and secret society.

Gradually, as the autumn deepened, the shop began to fill with people, and the old till made sounds it had not made in years. Children paused on their way to school to press their noses to the glass and watch the grey cat sleeping among the paperbacks, and a surprising number of them returned later with coins in their fists. Tessa, who had arrived with a plan to leave, found that she was making plans for the following week.

Daniel appeared one morning carrying a beautiful window seat that he had made himself from old oak, and he set it in the bay without a word of explanation. A small card tied to the cushion explained how to care for the wood, and Daniel passed it hurriedly to Poppy, who read it aloud in a ringing voice. Tessa saw the fleeting, tightened look on his face, and in that instant she understood something she had been half suspecting for weeks.

When Poppy had gone home, Tessa asked him, as gently as she knew how, whether reading was something he found difficult. He was quiet for a long time before admitting that the words slid and swam on the page, that the teachers at school had called him lazy, and that the other children had laughed until he stopped trying. He had grown into a man who could build anything with his hands and who hid, behind skill and silence, a wound that had never entirely healed.

Tessa did not offer sympathy, for she could see that he would have found it unbearable, and she did not suggest that he could simply try harder. Instead she took a piece of chalk, wrote on a small blackboard that every Thursday evening she would read aloud by the stove, and propped it up beside the door where he must see it. Daniel looked at the board for a moment, then at her, and said that he might come, if he happened to be passing.

On the first Thursday the shop was fuller than she had ever seen it, with neighbours carrying their own chairs and cushions and the old stove glowing like a small sun. Daniel slipped in late and took a seat at the very back, as though he hoped no one would notice him, and Tessa began to read in a clear, unhurried voice. Whenever she glanced up, she found him listening with an expression of such open and uncomplicated happiness that she lost her place on the page twice.

Afterwards they walked together along the harbour wall, where the sea was black and the lights of the fishing boats rocked like distant candles. Tessa confessed that she had left the city because she was exhausted by a life of working all day in rooms full of people who never really spoke to one another. For a long while they stood side by side in comfortable silence, and neither felt any urgent need to fill it.

Without quite understanding when it had started, Tessa discovered that she was counting the hours until Thursday, and that her week had begun to arrange itself around those evenings. Mrs Boyle, who noticed everything and forgave nothing, remarked over a plate of warm scones that Tessa had gone remarkably pink whenever a certain carpenter was mentioned. Tessa denied it with great dignity and then spent the next ten minutes pretending to be absorbed in the cat.

Late one night in November a ferocious storm lifted the corner of the shop's roof like the lid of a tin, and rain came hammering down onto the shelves. Daniel was the first to arrive, his coat pulled over his pyjamas, and within minutes half the lane had poured through the door to carry armfuls of books to dry places upstairs and next door. By the time the worst was over, there was a chain of neighbours stretching from the back room to the tearoom, passing the stock of a lifetime from hand to hand in the dark.

At dawn every chair, table and windowsill in the shop was spread with open books, steaming gently before the fire as though the paper itself were exhaling. Tessa and Daniel, soaked and shivering and giddy with exhaustion, stood side by side and carefully turned the pages of a damp atlas. When their fingers met over the corner of a map, neither of them moved away, and the silence stretched until the bang of Mrs Boyle's tea tray at the door made them both jump.

While clearing the last of Silas's belongings from his old rolltop desk, Tessa noticed that one drawer would not close properly, and she knelt to see what was blocking it. Pushed to the very back, wedged against the wood as though it had been waiting for her to look, was an envelope bearing her own name in the thin, upright hand she had come to know so well. She carried it to the window seat with trembling fingers and sat for a minute before she could bring herself to open it.

His letter was short, and it spoke to her as though they had known each other all her life. A shop, he wrote, is a kind of promise to strangers, and she should keep that promise only for as long as it made her happy, never out of duty or guilt. At the very end he added, with a flash of the humour she was beginning to adore, that Daniel Reyes would pretend he needed no help from anyone, and that she was to help him anyway.

The following afternoon Tessa climbed the lane to Daniel's workshop, where the air was sweet with sawdust and a half-finished cradle stood on the bench in a pool of sunlight. Rather shyly, and with his eyes fixed on a chisel, he asked whether she might recommend a book that he could manage to read, one that would not make him feel foolish. She chose a short, warm-hearted novel in generous print and placed it in his hands as carefully as though she were handing him something living.

Along with the book she gave him a sheet of pale blue plastic to lay over the page, a trick that some readers find calms the restless lines, though she was careful to promise nothing. Each evening he sat beside his stove and worked through a paragraph or two, tracing the words with his finger, stopping, returning, beginning again with a stubbornness that she found astonishing. Tessa, who had translated whole novels without noticing the effort, watched him labour over a single page and felt something shift deep in her chest.

One bright afternoon Daniel walked into the shop holding the book against his chest, and announced in a voice that was not quite steady that he had finished the first chapter. Tessa put the kettle on, bought a cake from the bakery without any particular excuse, and sat down with him at the little table in the window. They said very little over the tea, but the quality of the silence had altered, and she knew that both of them had noticed.

As autumn ripened, the oaks above the harbour burned yellow and gold, and the leaves came tumbling down the cobbles of Lantern Lane and drifted into the shop doorway. The takings had improved beyond anything Tessa had dared hope, and a respectable portion of the old debt had been paid. Yet when she sat down with her accounts, the arithmetic remained unforgiving, and the figure at the bottom of the page was still a long, long way from the one she needed.

Late one evening, sketching idly on the back of a receipt, Tessa found herself drawing the lane as it might look on a night of festival, with lanterns strung from window to window and stalls beneath every doorway. If books were the heart of the lane, she reasoned, then the lane should celebrate them in public, with readings, music and every single lamp burning, and bring the whole county to see. By the time the idea had a name, Lantern Night, she was grinning at the paper like a child.

To her astonishment, the neighbours took up the idea with an enthusiasm that bordered on the alarming. The baker promised cakes by the hundred, the florist offered garlands for every doorway, the schoolteacher volunteered a choir of pupils, and Mrs Boyle declared that she would serve tea to a thousand people if it killed her. Within days the lane had become a hive of whispered plans and measuring tapes, and Tessa, who had never before organised so much as a picnic, felt carried along on a warm tide.

Hoping to persuade him to lend his name to the festival, Tessa went to Mr Hargrove's office, where she delivered her proposal with every ounce of eloquence she possessed. He heard her out in a stony silence, then shook his head with a thin, patient smile and informed her that a shop is not a charity, and that dreams do not pay rent. She left the building in such a rage that Daniel, waiting outside, had to take her arm and steer her gently home.

Halfway down the lane he stopped beneath one of his grandfather's lamps and, with his gaze fixed on the glowing glass, confessed the fear that he had never spoken aloud. If the lane were sold and the hotel built, he said, the lamps would go dark for good, and sixty years of his family's quiet work would end with him. Tessa laid her hand over his, understanding at last that he was fighting for something far larger than a single shop.

Frost had settled over Port Hollin, and the lamps along the lane glowed like small moons in the cold clear air. Beneath the nearest one, Daniel took Tessa's gloved hand in both of his, and when she looked up at him, a little breathless, he kissed her so gently that she was not entirely sure it had happened. She stood smiling in the lamplight long after he had gone, feeling as though the whole street had been lit especially for her.

The very next day Marcus telephoned again, brisk and charming, to say that he must have her answer by the end of the week or the post would go to somebody else. Tessa put down the receiver with her heart beating hard, and it struck her, with a small cold shock, that she had not breathed a single word of the offer to Daniel. She told herself that she would explain it that evening, when the moment was right, and she did not notice how easily the moment slipped past.

Early on Friday Daniel came into the shop carrying a warm loaf from the baker, found her laptop lying open on the counter, and glanced at the glowing screen. He read the first line of the email, slowly and with effort, and the colour left his face as he took in the words job, salary and city. Tessa, coming down the stairs, saw him standing motionless with the loaf in his hands and knew at once what he had seen.

He told her, in a quiet, level voice that frightened her more than shouting would have done, that she ought to accept the post, because she deserved a far larger life than anything that this small lane could offer. Tessa, hurt and furious, replied that he had no right to decide her future for her and that he had made up his mind without even asking what she wanted. Within minutes they were both saying things they did not mean, and Daniel was walking out into the cold with the loaf still forgotten on the counter.

That night she sat on the window seat with the cat in her lap and the box of Silas's notes open beside her, reading them one by one as though they might give her an answer. Near the bottom, in faded blue ink that had almost vanished, she found a note that said simply that home is not a place but a lamp somebody leaves burning for you. She read it three times, then looked out of the window at the lane, where Daniel's lamps glowed in the dark all the way up the hill.

In the morning, before she could lose her nerve, Tessa telephoned Marcus Vale and told him, with sincere thanks, that she would not be taking the job. She added that she would be delighted to go on translating for his authors, and that she saw no reason why she could not do it just as well from a small bookshop at the top of a hill. There was a pause, a dry laugh, and a promise to send her the next manuscript, and she put down the telephone feeling suddenly as light as a leaf.

On the evening of Lantern Night the whole of Port Hollin seemed to have climbed the hill, and the lane glittered with paper lanterns, stalls heaped with books, and the smell of hot cakes and wood smoke. The choir sang beneath the shop window, Mrs Boyle bustled about with a tray, and strangers from the next county wandered from stall to stall with their arms full of paperbacks. Tessa smiled and greeted everyone, yet through it all her eyes kept searching the crowd for one tall figure, and he did not come.

Mr Hargrove arrived in his stiff grey coat and stood at the edge of the crowd with his hands clasped behind him, looking about with the bewilderment of a man who has wandered into someone else's dream. When old Tobias Finch rose to read a poem in his cracked, deep voice, the whole lane fell silent, and the landlord, almost without thinking, picked up a book from the nearest stall. A small folded note slipped out of its pages and fell at his feet, and he bent to pick it up with a stiff, uncertain hand.

It was a note from Silas, written many years earlier for a man who might one day be ready to be kind, and it spoke of friendship, and of a wife whom they had both loved. Mr Hargrove read it twice, took out a handkerchief, and then crossed the lane to Tessa with a face that she barely recognised. He told her gruffly that the shop would be offered a fair and lasting lease, and that the lamps of Lantern Lane would belong to the lane for as long as anyone wished to light them.

As the church clock struck nine, a tall figure appeared at the bottom of the lane and began to walk steadily up the hill through the lantern light, a folded sheet of paper in his hand. Daniel stopped in front of Tessa, in full view of the crowd, and told her that the page had taken him three weeks to write, that the spelling was dreadful, and that he meant to read it to her anyway. His voice shook at the start, but he read every word, slowly and bravely, and in those words he said that he was afraid, that he was sorry, and that he loved her.

Tessa told him that she had refused the job days ago, and that she had no intention of going anywhere, ever, unless he were coming with her. Then she took one end of the long brass pole and Daniel took the other, and together they lit the lamps from the bottom of the lane to the top, while the whole of Port Hollin laughed and cheered in the glow. When the last flame caught, the sound that rose from the crowd was so loud that the cat, asleep in the window, opened one eye in mild reproach.

By the following spring, a handsome new sign had been painted above the door in Daniel's neat hand, with Poppy supervising every stroke, and it read Wren Books in letters of blue and gold. Inside, Daniel sat on the window seat with a thick novel on his knee, a blue sheet over the page and a look of deep contentment on his face, while the cat dozed beside him in the sun. Behind the counter, Tessa smiled as she slipped a fresh note into a book for a stranger she had not yet met, and for the first time in her life she knew that she was exactly where she belonged.
